summary: Jesus sends a larger group ahead in pairs as harvest workers and vulnerable guests. They bring peace, receive hospitality, heal, and announce God's kingdom; rejection still means the kingdom has come near. Returning with joy over spiritual authority, they are redirected toward belonging to God. Jesus rejoices in the Spirit and blesses what disciples see. A legal expert's question about eternal life becomes a question about neighbor; Jesus's Samaritan story shifts the task from defining the eligible neighbor to becoming one through costly mercy. In a village, Martha welcomes Jesus but is pulled apart by anxious service, while Mary sits as a disciple and listens.
whyItMatters: Mission is neither domination nor self-sufficiency: it enters as peace, dependence, healing, and shared table. Neighbor is a practiced identity rather than a boundary category, and even good service becomes distorted when anxiety prevents presence to the person being served.

context.author: The anonymous author, traditionally identified as Luke, opening the journey with mission, revelation, Samaritan mercy, and a women-discipleship scene
context.audience: Theophilus and a wider Greek-reading audience; the chapter addresses hospitality, rejection, religious boundaries, service, and listening
context.date: Commonly dated around AD 80–90, after AD 70; earlier dates in the 60s and later ones into the early second century are defended
context.setting: Towns on the way to Jerusalem, a dangerous road from Jerusalem to Jericho, an inn, and Martha's village home
context.literaryForm: Mission discourse, woes, thanksgiving, legal dialogue, exemplary story, and household scene

outline.heading: Seventy(-two) sent as workers and guests
outline.note: Seventy others are sent two by two with no purse; they say 'Peace be to this house' and heal the sick

outline.heading: Woes, representation, and return with joy
outline.note: Woe to Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum; the seventy return with joy that demons obey; he says rejoice that their names are written in heaven

outline.heading: Jesus rejoices in the Spirit and blesses witnesses
outline.note: Jesus thanks the Father for revealing things to little children, then tells the disciples many prophets and kings wanted to see what they see

outline.heading: Law, eternal life, and the merciful Samaritan
outline.note: A lawyer asks about eternal life; Jesus tells of a robbed man passed by a priest and Levite, then cared for by a Samaritan

outline.heading: Martha's welcome, anxious service, and Mary's listening
outline.note: Martha, distracted with serving, asks him to tell Mary to help; he says 'one thing is needed' and Mary has chosen the good part

keyVerses.text: He answered, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your strength, and with all your mind; and your neighbor as yourself.”
keyVerses.why: Jesus and the legal expert agree that Torah joins whole-person love of God to neighbor-love.

keyVerses.text: Now which of these three do you think seemed to be a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?”
keyVerses.why: Jesus turns a boundary question into a vocation: neighbor is what mercy makes someone become.

keyVerses.text: but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.”
keyVerses.why: A woman receives the enduring place of a disciple listening at the teacher's feet.

questions.question: Were seventy or seventy-two disciples sent?
questions.answer: Ancient Greek witnesses preserve both numbers, and both carry scriptural resonance: the peoples listed in Genesis 10 number seventy in the Hebrew text, and the Greek version adds and drops some names. Modern critical editions often print seventy-two. The mission's breadth and paired sending do not depend on settling the number.

questions.question: What is a ‘son of peace’?
questions.answer: It is a Semitic-style expression for a person worthy of the offered peace, not a biological title or secret class. The greeting is real gift and test: if welcomed it rests there; if not, it returns. Mission offers peace without forcing acceptance.

questions.question: Why tell workers to eat whatever is set before them?
questions.answer: Travelers depend on hosts and must not shop for superior hospitality or impose unnecessary status distinctions. Receiving table fellowship supports mission across households and cultures. The command also makes the worker economically vulnerable rather than a patron controlling the host.

questions.question: Did Jesus literally see Satan fall from heaven?
questions.answer: The saying interprets the disciples' successful liberation as the collapse of satanic authority. It may describe visionary perception, primordial defeat, or an apocalyptic image of what their mission enacts. Luke's emphasis lands on authority under Jesus and then on humility: rejoice that your names are written in heaven, not in power over spirits.

questions.question: Why are priest and Levite in the story, and were they simply avoiding impurity?
questions.answer: The text never states their motives. Torah barred a priest from defiling himself for the dead (Leviticus 21:1), so purity explanations are possible but insufficient; Torah also commands neighbor-love (10:27). Their honored religious roles heighten the failure to act, while the socially suspect Samaritan becomes the one who fulfills neighbor-love.

questions.question: Why is ‘Good Samaritan’ a sharper phrase than it sounds today?
questions.answer: Judeans and Samaritans disputed where God should be worshiped (John 4:20), and hostility could be real (9:53; John 4:9). Jesus selects the boundary figure the hearer might least expect, then makes him the compassionate agent. The story is not praise for generic niceness; it demands costly mercy across inherited enmity.

questions.question: Is Martha condemned for serving?
questions.answer: No. She welcomes Jesus, and her serving, diakonia in Greek, is honorable in Luke, where Jesus says ‘I am among you as one who serves’ (22:27). The problem is that she is distracted, literally ‘drawn around,’ by much service and anxious enough to enlist Jesus against Mary. Jesus addresses her tenderly and protects attentive discipleship from being consumed by performance.

questions.question: What is radical about Mary sitting at Jesus's feet?
questions.answer: Sitting at a teacher's feet is a disciple posture. Jesus affirms Mary's place and says it will not be taken away. The scene is not an argument that contemplation belongs to women and service to men; both are discipleship practices ordered around Jesus.

glossary.def: Image for people ready to receive God's kingdom and the urgent need for workers.
Prophetic warning and lament over refusal, not permission for disciples to retaliate.
Member of a community centered on the Torah and Mount Gerizim, with a contested relationship to Judeans.
Service or ministry; honorable work that can still become anxious and misdirected.
